pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally — including ×0 and ×1, ÷1, and multiplying three numbers by choosing a useful pair first.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including: multiplying by 0 and 1; dividing by 1; multiplying together three numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.5 (properties as strategies) and 3.OA.7 (fluency using strategies); the identity/zero properties appear in the properties-of-operations table.
• Operational details — this consolidates mental strategy: (a) place value (40×6 = 4 tens ×6 = 240); (b) the special cases — ×1 leaves a number unchanged (identity), ×0 gives 0 (zero property), ÷1 leaves a number unchanged — taught with meaning (1 group of n; n groups of 1; 0 groups) not as rules; (c) associativity/commutativity to reorder three factors into an easy pair first (2×7×5 → 2×5×7 = 10×7 = 70). The habit is to LOOK for the easy route before calculating. Note ÷0 is not required here (and is undefined) — keep to ×0, ×1, ÷1.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): 40×6 mentally via place value; state ×1 and ×0 results. Tier B (age 8–9): reorder three numbers to find an easy pair (2×9×5). Tier C (age 9): explain WHY ×0=0 and ×1/÷1 leave a number unchanged using the groups meaning.
bestPractices: Teach ×0, ×1, ÷1 through the equal-groups meaning (1 group of n = n; n groups of 1 = n; 0 groups = 0) so they're understood, not memorised as rules.
Build the habit of scanning three-factor products for the easiest pair to combine first (make a ten, or a known fact), justified by commutativity/associativity.
Use place-value reasoning for mental ×÷ with multiples of ten (40×6 = 24 tens = 240).
Verbalise the chosen strategy each time ('I'll pair the 2 and 5 to make 10') to make flexible method-choice explicit.
Keep ÷0 out of scope and, if raised, address it meaningfully (you can't make groups that share nothing / it's undefined).
keyRepresentations: Equal-groups images for the identity/zero cases (1 group of n; n groups of 1; 0 groups)
Rearrangeable factor tiles for three-number products (regroup to make a ten)
Place-value counters for × multiples of ten
Number line / known-fact chains for derived facts
commonMisconceptions: Thinking ×0 gives the other number, or ×1 doubles/changes it, when treated as rote rules.
Believing multiplication always makes a number bigger (so ×1 or later × a fraction surprises).
Not reordering three factors, so multiplying left-to-right the hard way.
Miscounting place value in 40×6 (getting 24 instead of 240).

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: multiply and divide mentally using place value, known and derived facts, including the special cases ×0, ×1 and ÷1, and multiplying three numbers by choosing a useful pair first. The goal is flexible strategy choice — looking for the easy route before calculating — with the identity/zero cases understood through the equal-groups meaning rather than memorised as rules. Note: ÷0 is out of scope and is undefined; keep to ×0, ×1, ÷1.

activities.title: Reorder three factors to find the easy pair
feedback: If a learner ploughs left to right or stalls, prompt: 'Is there a pair that makes a ten, or a fact you already know?' Then let them try pairing 2 and 5.
If they doubt that reordering is allowed, have them compute two orders (e.g. 2 × 7 × 5 and 5 × 2 × 7) and confirm both give 70.
When they verbalise the chosen strategy ('I'll pair the 2 and 5 to make 10'), affirm that naming the plan is the skill being built.
activities.rationale: Building the habit of scanning three-factor products for the easiest pair, justified by commutativity/associativity, makes flexible method-choice explicit. An optional manipulable surface — three draggable number tiles feeding one live product readout, where pairing 2 and 5 fuses them into a glowing 10 while the total never changes as tiles are shuffled — can make the invariance felt; this interaction is an example, not a requirement.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including ×0 and ×1, ÷1, and multiplying three numbers.
Properties of operations (including identity and zero) are used as strategies for fluent mental calculation.
The identity/zero cases should be taught through the equal-groups meaning; reordering three factors for an easy pair uses commutativity/associativity.
learnerActions: Work out 2 × 7 × 5 in your head, saying aloud which two numbers you multiply first and why.
Try pairing 2 and 5 first to make 10, then multiply by 7 to get 70; compare this with going left to right (2 × 7 = 14, then × 5 = 70).
Check that different orders give the same total: is 2 × 7 × 5 the same as 5 × 2 × 7? Explain why you are allowed to reorder.
Repeat with 2 × 9 × 5 and 4 × 3 × 5, each time scanning for a pair that makes a ten or a known fact first.
activities.intendedInsight: Reordering factors is always allowed (commutativity/associativity) and the total stays the same — but some orderings turn a fiddly three-number product into a single known fact, so it pays to look for the friendly pair before calculating.

activities.title: Understand ×1, ×0 and ÷1 through groups
feedback: If a learner says 8 × 0 = 8 or 8 × 1 = 0, act it out with counters: 8 groups of 0 is nothing (0); 8 groups of 1 is 8. Contrast directly with adding 0.

If a learner expects ×1 to make the number bigger (believing multiplication always increases a number), use the single-group picture: one group of 8 is still 8, so multiplying by 1 changes nothing — multiplication does not always make a number larger.

If they confuse ÷1 with halving or with ÷0, return to the division picture: 8 ÷ 1 is one whole group (or groups of one), so you get everything back, 8. ÷0 is different — you cannot share 8 among zero groups, and no number of groups of 0 makes 8, so it is left undefined and out of scope.
Praise explanations that reference groups rather than restating a rule.
activities.rationale: Teaching the identity/zero cases through equal-groups meaning targets the common rote-rule confusions (×0 gives the other number; ×1 changes it) and the belief that multiplying always increases a number. Optional tap-to-reveal panels pairing each case (×1, ×0, ÷1) with its groups picture and a 'why' flap can anchor the meaning.
sourceClaims: The identity/zero cases should be taught through the equal-groups meaning; reordering three factors for an easy pair uses commutativity/associativity.
Properties of operations (including identity and zero) are used as strategies for fluent mental calculation.
learnerActions: Lay out counters to show 8 × 1 as 'one group of 8' and '8 groups of 1'; confirm both give 8.
Show 8 × 0 as '8 groups of nothing' — every group is empty, so the total is 0.
Show 8 ÷ 1 as one whole group of 8 (or sharing 8 into groups of one) and confirm the result is still 8.
Say in your own words why n × 1 = n, why n × 0 = 0, and why n ÷ 1 = n.
Contrast 8 × 0 with 8 + 0: adding 0 leaves 8, but 0 groups of 8 (or 8 groups of 0) is nothing — notice the roles are different.
activities.intendedInsight: ×1 and ÷1 leave a number unchanged because you have one whole group (or share into groups of one), and ×0 gives 0 because there are no groups (or every group is empty) — these are meanings to be seen, not rules to memorise.

activities.title: Scale with place value for multiples of ten
feedback: If a learner answers 24 (ten times too small), prompt: '4 what times 6? Four tens — so 24 tens, which is 240.'
Have them restate the known fact (4 × 6 = 24) and then re-apply the ten-times adjustment rather than reteaching from scratch when the method is sound but the number slips.
activities.rationale: Place-value reasoning for mental ×÷ with multiples of ten addresses the frequent error of multiplying the tens digit as ones. Place-value counters can make the 'tens' unit concrete; restating the underlying known fact models the known-fact chain for derived facts.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including ×0 and ×1, ÷1, and multiplying three numbers.
learnerActions: Work out 40 × 6 mentally by reasoning '4 tens × 6 = 24 tens = 240'; say the 'tens' name aloud as you go.
Explain how knowing 4 × 6 = 24 helps you get 40 × 6.
Try 30 × 7 and 50 × 8 the same way, keeping the place-value name attached to each digit.
Check your answer is sensible: 40 × 6 is exactly ten times 4 × 6, so 240, not 24.
activities.intendedInsight: A known fact can be scaled by place value: 40 × 6 is ten times 4 × 6, so the answer is 240, not 24 — keeping the 'tens' label attached prevents losing the place value.

activities.title: Consolidate and check reasoning
feedback: For a correct strategy with an arithmetic slip, do not reteach — ask the learner to re-state the known fact and re-apply the adjustment.
If explanations fall back on rules, redirect to the groups picture or to checking that two orderings give the same total.
Watch for the persistent 7 × 0 = 7 and 7 × 1 = 0 confusions and address them with counters (7 groups of 0 is 0; 7 groups of 1 is 7).
activities.rationale: Checking mental results and strategy choice consolidates fluency and surfaces reasoning that a bare answer hides, including asking learners to justify ×1 = n and why reordering is allowed (properties of operations as strategies). A response format (multiple-choice for the easiest pairing, fill-in for ×0/×1/÷1, a 'why' explanation) can be used during teaching to verify and prompt justification; recognition formats verify understanding rather than, on their own, building independent strategy construction.
sourceClaims: Properties of operations (including identity and zero) are used as strategies for fluent mental calculation.
learnerActions: Decide which pair you would multiply first in 2 × 9 × 5 and say why.
Give the results for 7 × 0, 7 × 1 and 7 ÷ 1, and explain each using the groups meaning.
Answer: why does any number × 1 equal that same number?
Explain why you are free to reorder the factors in a three-number product.
activities.intendedInsight: Strategy choice and the special-case results are things you can state and justify, not just compute — being able to explain why confirms genuine understanding.

constraints: Keep ÷0 out of scope; if a learner raises it, explain meaningfully that you cannot share 8 among zero groups, and no number of groups of 0 ever makes 8 — so 8 ÷ 0 is undefined — rather than giving a number.
Teach ×0, ×1 and ÷1 through the equal-groups meaning so they are understood, not memorised; rules learned by rote without meaning can leave learners prone to the ×0 = n and ×1 = 0 confusions.
Multiplication does not always make a number larger: ×1 leaves it unchanged and ×0 gives 0. Expect and address this surprise rather than letting 'multiplying makes it bigger' stand.

Recognition-only formats (choosing the right answer, filling a blank) verify results and can prompt justification, but do not by themselves elicit independent mental strategy construction; pair them with learners computing and explaining their own method.

Tap-to-reveal panels and draggable factor tiles are optional scaffolds that make invariance and group meaning concrete; they illustrate the mechanism and are not required for the learning, and a fixed worked example can still teach the same meaning.
The additive identity (adding 0) and multiplicative zero (×0) behave differently; contrast them explicitly so learners do not carry over 'adding 0 leaves it unchanged' to multiplication.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

In the source material, two of three cited sources (CCSS-M and NCETM) are marked verified:false; treat the identity/zero and reordering teaching principles as informed guidance, not independently confirmed efficacy claims.
The source misconception 'multiplication always makes a number bigger (so ×1 surprises)' is addressed in the ×1/×0/÷1 activity feedback and as a constraint.

The source's artefact-fit note that '3D adds cost without insight' for these planar numeric strategies is a catalog ranking, not an established pedagogical law; it has been dropped rather than asserted. A screen model and physical counters offer different experiences; neither is claimed universally necessary.
The added example 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 is agent-proposed and not from the source example set; it is arithmetically correct but untested as an item.
The ÷1 feedback was clarified to state the division model (one whole group / groups of one gives everything back) consistently before contrasting with the undefined ÷0.

probeDeeper: For 2 × 7 × 5, which two did you multiply first, and why those?
What is 8 × 0 — and why? What about 8 × 1?
How does knowing 4 × 6 help you with 40 × 6?
Is 2 × 7 × 5 the same as 5 × 2 × 7? Why can you reorder them?
assess.correctAnswer: 240 (4×6 = 24, then ×10 for the tens); 70 (reorder to 2×5 = 10, ×7 = 70); 8×0 = 0; 8×1 = 8. The teacher watches for place-value scaling, using commutativity/associativity to pick an easy pair, and correct, reasoned handling of the identity/zero cases.

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks n × 0 = n (or n × 1 = 0) — confuses the roles of the additive and multiplicative identities/zero
errorPatterns.nextMove: ground in groups: 8 groups of 0 is nothing (0); 8 groups of 1 is 8; act it out with counters, contrasting with adding 0.

errorPatterns.pattern: does not reorder the three numbers — multiplies left to right (2×7 = 14, ×5 = 70) missing the easier 2×5 pairing, or stalls
errorPatterns.nextMove: show associativity/commutativity let you pick the friendliest pair first; look for pairs making 10s.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child computes the awkward way or loses track; doesn't spot the 2×5 = 10

errorPatterns.pattern: for 40 × 6 multiplies the tens digit as ones (answer 24) forgetting the place value
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason 4 tens × 6 = 24 tens = 240; keep the 'tens' name attached to the digit.
do not reteach; have the child re-state the known fact and re-apply the adjustment.

responseLevels.gap: confuses ×0/×1, multiplies tens as ones, or cannot handle a three-number product.
responseLevels.full: scales by place value, reorders three factors to pick friendly pairs (associativity/commutativity), and reasons correctly about ×0 and ×1.
responseLevels.partial: handles place-value scaling but doesn't reorder to find easy pairs, or is inconsistent on the identity/zero cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these in their head, saying how: 40 × 6; then 2 × 7 × 5 (watch whether they reorder to pair 2 and 5); and slip in 8 × 0 and 8 × 1. Watch the place-value reasoning, the choice of a useful pair, and how they treat the ×0 and ×1 cases.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three-number product reveals whether the child flexibly reorders (2×5 first) or ploughs left to right; the ×0 and ×1 items catch the persistent 8×0 = 8 and 8×1 = 0 confusions. Watching the mental strategy exposes reasoning that a bare answer hides.
